title: Multiplication by $n$ is surjective with finite kernel
statement:
Let $A$ be an abelian variety
over a field $k$, and let $n\geq1$. Then the map $[n]$ of
[def-sc-mult-n] is a surjective homomorphism of
group schemes, and its kernel
$A[n]$ is a finite group scheme over $k$.

proof.text:
*Reference: Stacks Project, Groupoid Schemes, Proposition
39.9.11 (3) and (5), [Tag 03RP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03RP), whose proof is Lemma 39.9.8,
[Tag 0BFG](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BFG).*
By [lem-sc-mult-n-finite-kernel], $[n]$ is a finite homomorphism of group
schemes and its kernel $A[n]$ is a finite group scheme over $k$.

*Surjectivity.* By [def-sc-abelian-variety], $A$ is proper, smooth and connected over $k$; properness gives separatedness and finite type. The identity section makes $A$ nonempty. By [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization], $A$ is geometrically integral, hence irreducible and reduced [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Apply [lem-sc-image-subgroup] to the homomorphism $[n]$ of [lem-sc-mult-n-homomorphism]: its scheme-theoretic image $H\hookrightarrow A$ is a closed subgroup scheme of finite type over $k$, and the induced $g:A\to H$ is surjective. The map $g$ is finite: on any affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $A$, the image $H\cap U$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)$; because $[n]$ is finite by step 1, $[n]^{-1}(U)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ for a finite $R$-module $B$. The factorization makes $I$ act by zero on $B$, so $B$ is finite over $R/I$. Thus [lem-sc-finite-surjective-dimension] gives equal finite topological Krull dimensions for $H$ and $A$. If the closed set $|H|$ were proper in irreducible $|A|$, every chain of irreducible closed subsets of $|H|$ could be extended by $|A|$, giving $\dim H<\dim A$ by [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], a contradiction. Hence $|H|=|A|$. On each affine $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq A$, the ideal $I$ defining $H\cap U$ lies in every prime of $R$, so it lies in the nilradical; since $A$ is reduced, $I=0$. Thus $H=A$ as schemes, and the surjection $g$ proves that $[n]:A\to A$ is surjective.
